title: Why Do Photos of You Look Wrong?

fin.small: Sources: Mita, Dermer and Knight, J. Personality and Social Psychology 35(8), 1977; Amestoy et al., Frontiers in Psychology 1:39, 2010.

parts: The face you see in the mirror is not the face your friends see.
Stay to the end for the numbers, and the leading idea behind them.
A mirror flips you left to right.
And no face is perfectly symmetrical, so the flipped one really looks different.
In 1977, researchers tested which version of their own face people liked: normal or flipped.
People tended to pick the flipped one. Their friends, the normal one.
But why would your own friends disagree with you?
In 2010, a team in Bordeaux tested it with thirty-eight adults. Seventy-one percent preferred their mirror face.
And seventy-six percent preferred the normal photo of their friend.
Leading idea: we prefer what we see most. You see your mirror face. They don't.
Our reading: maybe that photo isn't wrong. It's just unfamiliar. Subscribe for the next one.
